title: Addressing Cascading Failures
subtitle: Break the feedback loops that turn overload into collapse
summary: Pip removes an overloaded replica and its peers fail next. Cascades reduce capacity while creating more work. The crew sheds load, preserves useful responses, bounds retries, and restores traffic only as recovering capacity can support it.

concepts.title: Positive feedback and reduced recovery capacity
concepts.body: Pip removes an overloaded replica and sends its traffic to already struggling peers. Slow requests retain threads and memory, reinforcing failure. Restarting replicas leave less capacity than before the incident. A fleet formerly serving 10,000 requests per second cannot recover at 9,000 with only a tenth healthy; Pip lowers load accordingly.

concepts.title: Load shedding, degradation, and deadlines
concepts.body: Pip skips optional enrichment to preserve useful search results. Load shedding rejects work before exhaustion; graceful degradation reduces work per useful response. Small queues, original deadlines, and propagated cancellation avoid serving requests after callers stop waiting. Pip tests these rarely used paths before an overload depends on them.

concepts.title: Retry budgets and randomized backoff
concepts.body: Pip finds three retrying layers allowing four attempts each. One user action can become sixty-four database attempts. Budgets limit total amplification, exponential backoff spaces attempts, and jitter prevents synchronized retries. Pip assigns retry ownership and explicit nonretryable signals so these complementary mechanisms work together.

concepts.title: Testing and recovering beyond the breaking point
concepts.body: Pip load-tests beyond failure and watches whether the service recovers. Gradual and sudden traffic, cold caches, restarts, and blackholed optional backends reveal hidden dependencies. During a cascade, Pip contains the trigger and admits enough traffic to warm surviving capacity gradually. Restarting everything could discard the very caches and capacity needed for recovery.

misconceptions.claim: Restoring the old request rate always restores service.
misconceptions.correction: Restart loops and cold caches can leave far less effective capacity, requiring a deeper temporary traffic reduction.

misconceptions.claim: Adding retries makes failure handling safer by default.
misconceptions.correction: Retries can be a positive feedback loop; limits, jitter, backoff, and ownership across layers are necessary.

scenario.title: Stop a retry cascade
scenario.context: A profile service slows, and three clients retry failed calls. CPU is rising from retries even though incoming traffic is flat.

options.label: Add jitter, limits, and a retry budget
options.benefit: Retry pressure becomes bounded and less synchronized.
options.cost: Some requests fail sooner and need a fallback.
options.consequence: The team caps retries per request and uses a process budget while repairing the dependency.

options.label: Increase every client timeout and retry count
options.benefit: Longer timeouts may tolerate a brief dependency pause.
options.cost: The cascade consumes more capacity and delays recovery.
options.consequence: The added retries deepen the overload and widen the outage.

scenario.debrief: The retries are adding load even though original demand is flat. Bound total retry traffic, add randomized backoff, and address the dependency’s trigger. Recovery may require temporarily reducing demand below its former safe level.

quiz.question: Why can a service remain unstable after demand returns below its former safe rate?
options: The original safe rate included all retries even during a crash loop
Failed and warming replicas leave less usable capacity than before
The configured capacity is unchanged, so recovery depends only on elapsed time
quiz.explanation: Recovery capacity can be much smaller than normal capacity.

quiz.question: What does a process-wide retry budget limit?
options: The total extra retry traffic generated by that process
The number of concurrent first attempts admitted to each backend
The maximum deadline for one failed logical request
quiz.explanation: An aggregate retry budget bounds amplification across many failing requests.

quiz.question: What should an overload test examine after crossing the breaking point?
options: Only the highest observed CPU value
Whether the request generator can send more traffic
Whether the service recovers as load falls and what reduction is required
quiz.explanation: Recovery can follow a different path from the initial rise in load.

exercise.title: Trace a cascade
exercise.prompt: Draw a feedback chain from one slow dependency to resource exhaustion. Specify how to break it and how to demonstrate recovery.
